classification.difficultyReason: Mentally rotate or reflect figures while checking size, boundary shape and internal segments; reject similar-looking figures with altered dimensions or markings.

questions.mappingNote: The task directly assesses congruent-figure recognition, including scale and internal segments, without requiring triangle congruence tests.
questions.methodNote: Move a complete figure by translations, rotations and reflections to test exact coincidence. Congruent figures have the same size and shape and matching corresponding features.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognise equal size and shape under rotation and reflection while checking internal segments.

classification.difficultyReason: Match corresponding vertices, sides and angles in two supplied congruent figures.

questions.mappingNote: Question 2 directly applies the paired-point, paired-interval and paired-angle notation demonstrated on page 2 and summarised on page 3.
questions.methodNote: Pair corresponding points by a translation, rotation or reflection that makes the figures coincide; pair intervals by their endpoints and angles by their ordered three-point names.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Match corresponding vertices, sides and angles in two supplied congruent figures.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply equal size and shape to everyday examples and recognise reflected or rotated letters and digits, allowing for printing size and approximate physical likeness.

questions.mappingNote: Each discussion item tests recognition of congruence through size, shape or a rigid transformation; no triangle congruence test is required.
questions.methodNote: Use the definition of congruence: figures coincide exactly after translations, rotations or reflections and have the same size and shape.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the definition of congruence to familiar objects and recognise reflections and rotations.

classification.difficultyReason: Match vertices from supplied angles and side markings, then translate those correspondences into ordered triangle names despite changes in orientation.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts directly assess congruence statements rather than formal triangle-test proofs. Part a uses right angles and Greek angle labels; b permits interchangeable base vertices; c uses all side ticks and angle labels; d uses the supplied angle and side correspondences.
questions.methodNote: Match paired vertices using equal angles and side markings; write triangle names in corresponding order. Translation, reflection and rotation preserve congruence.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Match explicitly marked corresponding vertices and write them in matching order.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise fixed-side rigidity and justify equal rope lengths by applying congruence tests to physical situations.

questions.mappingNote: Part a applies SSS to rigidity. Part b applies AAS using equal pole lengths, equal 20-degree angles and right angles under the explicitly added horizontal-ground assumption. Neither task requires trigonometry.
questions.methodNote: Page 8 establishes SSS and that three fixed sides determine the angles. Pages 9–11 explain matching sides, AAS and conclusions from corresponding sides of congruent triangles. Page 13 applies SSS with a common side; its final Example 5 conclusion contains triangle symbols where angle symbols are intended.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognise fixed-side rigidity and justify equal rope lengths by applying congruence tests to physical situations.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct a triangle from three sides and explain impossible side-length combinations using the triangle inequality; SSS is the closest available catalogue skill.

questions.mappingNote: Part a directly uses the taught ruler-and-compasses construction. Parts b and c infer and apply the triangle inequality. Congruent triangle tests is the closest supplied catalogue skill because the construction establishes a triangle from three specified sides.
questions.methodNote: Page 8 introduces SSS. Page 9 constructs a triangle by drawing a baseline and two circles centred at its endpoints, then joining a circle intersection to the endpoints. Question 2 develops the restriction on three side lengths through an unsuccessful construction.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct a triangle from three sides and explain impossible side-length combinations using the triangle inequality; SSS is the closest available catalogue skill.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct a triangle using two angles and a side, explain uniqueness using AAS, and reject impossible angle data.

questions.mappingNote: Part a uses the given base and its endpoint angles to construct intersecting rays, then invokes the locally named AAS test to explain equal measured lengths. Part b checks whether the two supplied angles can belong to a triangle. No trigonometric solution is introduced.
questions.methodNote: Page 10 states the triangle angle sum and defines AAS using two angles and a matching side. Page 11 demonstrates intersecting rays from the ends of a given base and explains the reflected congruent construction. Pages 11–12 conclude that matching sides of congruent triangles are equal. Page 9 establishes ruler-and-compasses construction as the local method.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct a triangle using two angles and a side, explain uniqueness using AAS, and reject impossible angle data.

classification.difficultyReason: Find missing angles, establish vertex correspondence and select SSS or AAS; crucially, reject the pair whose equal numerical sides occupy different corresponding positions.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a and d use three matching sides; b, c and f use two matching angles and a matching side; e tests whether the given equal sides actually correspond.
questions.methodNote: Page 8 states SSS and requires matching vertex order and test initials. Pages 9–10 match sides using opposite equal angles, use the triangle angle sum, and define AAS to include any matching side with two matching angles.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Match vertices from side and angle information, calculate missing angles where necessary, and distinguish an unequal matching side.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify matching vertices and an appropriate congruence test, supplying the common side in the joined figure, then infer the requested corresponding measurement.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a and c apply AAS and corresponding sides; part b applies SSS using the shared side PQ and then corresponding angles. This directly assesses congruent-triangle tests rather than construction or trigonometry.
questions.methodNote: Pages 8–11 establish SSS, matching vertices and the local AAS convention, including an equal matching side between the given angles. Page 12 Examples 3 and 4 first establish congruence, then use corresponding angles or sides to find an unknown. Page 13 explains a common side as the third equal pair for SSS.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify matching vertices, establish congruence using AAS or SSS, and deduce an unknown corresponding length or angle.

classification.difficultyReason: Organise marked equalities into SSS or AAS proofs with correct vertex order, then justify the target equality using corresponding elements.

questions.mappingNote: Part a applies Example 5's SSS proof pattern to three marked side pairs. Part b uses the two marked angle pairs and matching hypotenuses to establish AAS before concluding equality of corresponding sides. Formal congruence proof is the most advanced directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 8 establishes SSS and matching angles. Pages 9–11 explain matching sides and the local AAS convention, including a side between the supplied angles. Page 12 uses congruence to infer corresponding measurements. Page 13 Example 5 establishes congruence and then concludes equality of matching angles.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Establish congruence from marked givens, preserve corresponding vertex order and justify an equality of matching angles or sides.

classification.difficultyReason: Select SAS, RHS or AAS from marked diagrams and recognise insufficient non-included-angle data.

questions.mappingNote: Each part requires a correspondence-ordered congruence statement or recognition that congruence is not established.
questions.methodNote: Examples 6 and 7 supply SAS and RHS statement models; AAS uses the angle sum as in Example 2. Page 18 explains why non-included-angle data do not establish congruence.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Select SAS, RHS or AAS from marked diagrams and recognise insufficient non-included-angle data.

classification.difficultyReason: In the hardest part, combine equal component segments into equal whole sides and recognise the shared apex angle before forming a SAS proof and deducing corresponding sides.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts require a short congruence proof with reasons; part d first combines equal side segments.
questions.methodNote: Examples 8 and 9 establish congruence then conclude equality of matching angles or sides. Example 5 explains common sides.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Write congruence proofs using common sides, right angles and composite equal sides, then infer the requested equality.

classification.difficultyReason: Follow an explicitly supplied construction sequence, including constructing 30 degrees and drawing the specified arc; both intersections and the non-congruence conclusion are already supplied.

questions.mappingNote: The construction directly tests the limitation of SAS by producing both valid positions of the third vertex; congruent-triangle-tests is the closest supplied skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 15 requires the included angle for SAS. Page 18 demonstrates that two sides and a non-included angle can produce non-congruent triangles.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Constructs two triangles satisfying the same two sides and non-included angle to demonstrate why these conditions do not establish congruence.

classification.difficultyReason: Prove congruence and identify equal angles at the intersection, including recognising coincident rays in part c, then combine equality with a straight angle to establish perpendicularity.

questions.mappingNote: Each part follows the perpendicular-line proof structure of Example 12; the supplied givens select SAS or SSS.
questions.methodNote: Establish congruence, identify equal angles at the point on a straight line, and conclude that both are right angles.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Use triangle congruence and equal supplementary angles to establish perpendicular lines.

classification.difficultyReason: Follow the supplied proof stages, selecting SSS then SAS and transferring matching angles and sides between nested triangles. Equal supplementary angles establish perpendicularity; the circle case also requires recognising equal radii.

questions.mappingNote: The nested proof chains extend Example 12's congruence and equal-supplementary-angle method; the final circle result is proved rather than assumed.
questions.methodNote: Use SSS first, derive matching angles and right angles, then use SAS for the second pair of triangles and conclude matching lengths.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Link two congruence proofs, carrying intermediate angle results into conclusions about a kite and a common chord.

classification.difficultyReason: Explain the equal angles and use the converse of the isosceles triangle theorem to establish three equal sides.

questions.mappingNote: Question 2 proves the equilateral converse explicitly identified on teaching page 28.
questions.methodNote: Use the triangle angle sum and the theorem that sides opposite equal angles are equal.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Explain the equal angles and use the converse of the isosceles triangle theorem to establish three equal sides.

classification.difficultyReason: The perpendicular construction and triangle pair are supplied. Identify equal base angles, right angles and the common side to apply AAS, then infer equality of corresponding sides.

questions.mappingNote: This substitutes a perpendicular construction for the angle bisector used in the converse proof on page 27.
questions.methodNote: Use AAS with the given equal base angles, constructed right angles and common side; conclude corresponding sides are equal.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Use two equal angle pairs and a common side for AAS, then conclude the opposite sides are equal.

classification.difficultyReason: Devise an unprompted symbolic angle chain: express an isosceles base angle in terms of the apex angle, transfer it into the right triangle, and use complementary angles to establish the half-angle relationship.

questions.mappingNote: The assessed task is a proof of an isosceles-triangle angle property; no direct congruence proof is required.
questions.methodNote: Use the equal-base-angle theorem established on page 27 and triangle angle sums, as used in Example 13 on page 28.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combines equal base angles with the angle sum of a right-angled triangle to prove a general angle relationship.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate the verbal conditions into two right triangles, identify the bisected angles and common side, and choose AAS to prove the two original sides equal. No auxiliary construction beyond the stated bisector is needed.

questions.mappingNote: The final assessed conclusion is an isosceles-triangle property proved through congruence.
questions.methodNote: Apply AAS using the equal bisected angles, right angles and common side; conclude equality of matching sides, following the congruence proofs on page 27.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Requires naming a general configuration, establishing AAS congruence and concluding that two sides of the original triangle are equal.

classification.difficultyReason: Select SSS, SAS or AAS, match vertices and calculate a missing angle where needed.

questions.mappingNote: Part a uses the three matching sides from the SSS teaching on page 8; part b uses the included angle and two sides from page 15; part c follows the angle calculation and AAS sequence on pages 10–11. Page 6 supplies matching-vertex notation.
questions.methodNote: Write vertices in matching order, state the congruence test, and use the triangle angle sum before applying AAS when necessary.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Select SSS, SAS or AAS, match vertices and calculate a missing angle where needed.

classification.difficultyReason: Match vertices across differently oriented triangles and select SSS, RHS, SAS or AAS from the supplied givens.

questions.mappingNote: Part a matches three labelled side pairs; b matches marked right angles, hypotenuses and legs; c matches two sides and their included angle; d matches two angles and a corresponding side. All directly assess congruent triangle tests.
questions.methodNote: Page 6 establishes matching vertex order; page 8 gives SSS and appends the test to the statement; page 10 treats two equal angles and one matching side as AAS; page 15 requires the included angle for SAS; page 16 gives RHS.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Match vertices across differently oriented triangles and select SSS, RHS, SAS or AAS from the supplied givens.

classification.difficultyReason: Distinguish sufficient congruence markings from distractors and name matching vertices.

questions.mappingNote: Part a compares three side families; b rejects non-included-angle distractors; c requires the marked side to correspond to the same two angle families.
questions.methodNote: Match vertices in order; use SSS, SAS with the included angle, and the chapter's AAS convention for two angles and a matching side.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Distinguish sufficient congruence markings from distractors and name matching vertices.

classification.difficultyReason: Match vertices using marked sides and angles despite changed orientations, select the relevant congruence test, and transfer corresponding values. The right-triangle part adds a routine Pythagorean calculation before identifying the matching base.

questions.mappingNote: Part a uses SSS and corresponding angles; b uses SAS; c uses Pythagoras and RHS; d and e use two equal angles and a matching side. Applying triangle congruence is the principal assessed skill across the shared task.
questions.methodNote: Match vertices, sides and angles; establish SSS, SAS or AAS congruence, then use matching elements. Use the triangle angle sum in a. Page 16 supplies the RHS test and the rearranged Pythagorean calculation used in c.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Match corresponding sides and angles using SSS, SAS and AAS, and calculate a shorter side with Pythagoras’ theorem.

classification.difficultyReason: Justify a compass construction using SSS and conclude that corresponding angles are equal.

questions.mappingNote: The task requires a triangle-congruence proof and a conclusion about corresponding angles; prove-congruent-triangles is the directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Use matching vertex order, the SSS congruence test and equality of corresponding angles to justify the angle bisector.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Justify a compass construction using SSS and conclude that corresponding angles are equal.

classification.difficultyReason: Connect SSS and SAS proofs with corresponding sides, corresponding angles and supplementary angles to justify a perpendicular-bisector construction.

questions.mappingNote: The task requires a linked formal congruence proof, making prove-congruent-triangles the closest primary skill. Page 8 teaches SSS, page 9 equal-radius compass constructions, page 13 corresponding parts and common sides, and page 15 SAS.
questions.methodNote: Use equal construction radii and a common side for SSS; conclude matching angles are equal. Then use the included angle and common side for SAS, and finish with corresponding sides and supplementary equal angles.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Connect SSS and SAS proofs with corresponding sides, corresponding angles and supplementary angles to justify a perpendicular-bisector construction.

classification.difficultyReason: Interpret compass arcs as equal radii and follow the specified SSS-to-SAS proof chain. Transfer the first angle equality to the smaller triangles, then combine equal adjacent angles with a straight angle to prove perpendicularity.

questions.mappingNote: The task directly assesses a linked formal congruence proof, so prove-congruent-triangles is the primary skill. Page 8 supplies SSS, page 9 explains compass radii, page 13 demonstrates matching-angle conclusions and common sides, and page 15 supplies SAS.
questions.methodNote: Use equal compass radii and a common side for SSS, matching angles of congruent triangles, then two sides and their included angle for SAS. Equal adjacent angles on a straight line establish perpendicularity.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Links SSS and SAS proofs with corresponding angles and supplementary adjacent angles to justify a perpendicular construction.

classification.difficultyReason: Proves the isosceles base-angle property by comparing a triangle with itself using a reversed vertex correspondence.

questions.mappingNote: Page 15 states the SAS test; page 13 demonstrates deriving angle equality from congruence. This question applies those methods to one triangle with reversed vertex correspondence to prove the isosceles base-angle property.
questions.methodNote: Use two equal corresponding sides and their common included angle to establish SAS congruence, then conclude equality of matching angles.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Proves the isosceles base-angle property by comparing a triangle with itself using a reversed vertex correspondence.

classification.difficultyReason: Prove the converse isosceles-triangle property by matching a triangle to itself in reversed vertex order.

questions.mappingNote: The question proves the equal-base-angles converse for an isosceles triangle by comparing ABC with BAC; proving a triangle property is the most advanced directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Use the source's AAS test: two matching angles and a matching side establish congruence. Then deduce equality of matching sides, preserving the vertex correspondence.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Prove the converse isosceles-triangle property by matching a triangle to itself in reversed vertex order.

classification.difficultyReason: Critique an unjustified congruence claim by distinguishing a non-included angle from the included angle required by SAS.

questions.mappingNote: The task assesses criticism of a triangle-congruence proof. The midpoint and common side supply two side equalities, but the given base angles are non-included.
questions.methodNote: Match corresponding sides and angles, and apply SAS only when the equal angle is included between the two known equal sides.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Critique an unjustified congruence claim by distinguishing a non-included angle from the included angle required by SAS.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify why a purported congruence proof incorrectly applies SAS to a non-included angle.

questions.mappingNote: The task evaluates a purported formal congruence proof and its conclusion, matching constructing proofs using congruent triangles.
questions.methodNote: Page 15 defines SAS using the angle included between the equal sides and explicitly warns that a non-included angle cannot be used. Page 9 explains matching vertices, sides and angles.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify why a purported congruence proof incorrectly applies SAS to a non-included angle.

classification.difficultyReason: Reframe the unfamiliar congruence claim as uniqueness of a circle–ray intersection. The decisive unsignposted step is using the obtuse angle to place the ray's origin inside the circle, ruling out the usual two-triangle ambiguity and allowing only reflection.

questions.mappingNote: The response constructs a geometric justification of congruence rather than merely identifying a standard test; prove-congruent-triangles is the closest catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Use the source's circle-intersection construction and reflection reasoning. Page 18 explains the ambiguity of a non-included angle and explicitly refers to Challenge question 8.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Justifies a non-standard congruence test by explaining why an obtuse angle removes the ambiguous construction.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the supplied radius and isosceles-triangle hint to transfer the two labelled base angles to the split angle at P. Recognise that the large triangle's angle sum counts each angle twice, proving their sum is a right angle.

questions.mappingNote: The directly assessed result is the angle-in-a-semicircle theorem. The proof uses equal radii, isosceles base angles and the angle sum, without assuming the circle theorem being proved.
questions.methodNote: Page 26 defines isosceles triangles; page 27 establishes equality of their base angles. Page 28 demonstrates combining equal base angles with the triangle angle sum.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Proves the angle-in-a-semicircle theorem by combining two isosceles triangles with the angle sum of a triangle.

classification.difficultyReason: Beyond constructing extended altitudes, reinterpret the original three perpendicular relationships as altitudes of triangles containing H. This requires changing each point's role and recognising that the same lines prove concurrency in both acute and obtuse configurations.

questions.mappingNote: General geometrical reasoning is the closest catalogue match: the directly assessed proof concerns altitudes and concurrency rather than a triangle-congruence test.
questions.methodNote: Page 36 supplies the definitions of altitudes and orthocentre. Page 17 demonstrates perpendicular construction; page 23 discusses proving perpendicularity. The proof here directly reuses the three perpendicular relationships in the supplied definition.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct an exterior orthocentre and prove the reciprocal orthocentre relationships for four points.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the supplied congruence pairs to establish equal distances and interpret them as circle radii. Then independently select the triangles about the third midpoint, apply SSS and equal supplementary angles to prove perpendicularity, and identify the obtuse case for an exterior circumcentre.

questions.mappingNote: The central assessed task is a sequence of formal congruence proofs establishing the circumcentre properties, so prove-congruent-triangles is the closest catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Use SAS with midpoint equalities, common sides and included right angles; infer matching radii from congruence. For perpendicularity, follow Example 12 on page 23: SSS gives equal adjacent angles whose sum is a straight angle.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct a circumcentre and connect successive SAS and SSS proofs to equal radii and perpendicularity.
